Subject: Tenant isolation on private endpoints — who owns what for DNS + certs?

Hi Priyom,

Quick one from our infra team as we onboard a second environment behind our VPC peering with Redwood Private: we need to confirm who is responsible for the following items for each tenant / private domain:

- Creating the split-horizon DNS entries (customer-managed zone vs. Redwood-side stub zones)
- Provisioning and rotating TLS certificates for tenant-specific FQDNs (SAN vs. per-tenant cert)
- Handling SNI-based exceptions when requests must be routed to customer-owned proxies

Our security folks want a short, explicit matrix (owner: Acme vs Redwood) because this affects our audit evidence and automation flows. We also want to understand any proxy-routing exceptions (eg. when traffic for tenant-a.example.internal must be proxied to a customer appliance rather than the Redwood runtime) and how that changes cert responsibilities.

Can you share a concise owner matrix and call out the exceptional routing cases? If it's easier, we can hop on a quick 30-minute call today — we have a stub from NexusCloud (our edge proxy) who can join.

Thanks,
Alice Chen
Senior Cloud Platform Engineer
Acme Corp

Subject: Re: Tenant isolation on private endpoints — who owns what for DNS + certs?

Hi Alice — thanks for the clear ask. I put together a short responsibility matrix attached and a diagram that captures the two main routing patterns we see: 1) Redwood-terminated, tenant FQDN points to our private runtime and we provide/rotate certs; 2) Customer-proxied, FQDN points to customer appliance and the customer provides certs.

High-level summary here so it’s searchable from email:

- Split-horizon DNS: Prefer customer-managed private zone with a stub/NS delegation to a Redwood resolver where required. Owner: Customer (Acme) for zone creation; Redwood provides recommended records and an automation script.
- Tenant certs (Redwood-terminated): Redwood issues and rotates per-tenant certs (wildcard only if customer agrees in writing). We publish cert thumbprints to the agreed audit location. Owner: Redwood.
- Tenant certs (Customer-proxied): Customer retains cert responsibility and must present a cert signed by an accepted CA. Redwood will validate and pin the public cert (or accept OCSP stapling). Owner: Customer.
- SNI/proxy exceptions: When an inbound SNI must route to a customer appliance, the FQDN must resolve to the customer IP in the customer-controlled zone; Redwood will not terminate TLS for that FQDN. Owner: Customer for routing and certs; Redwood for interface-level ACLs and fallbacks.

I attached an editable matrix (tenant-dns-certificate-responsibility-matrix.xlsx) and a simple diagram (proxy-routing-exceptions-diagram.png).

Next steps I propose:
- Acme to confirm which tenants require customer-proxied routing vs Redwood termination.
- Monica / Karthik and I will validate any automation hooks (CSR exchange APIs, cert pinning format).
- If Nexus wants to join, let's do 30 minutes at 1:00pm PT.

If that all sounds good I can turn the matrix into a checklist for your SOC2 evidence.

—Priyom

Thanks Priyom — adding a few technical clarifications from the runtime side so the matrix has operational detail. Low-friction items first, then gotchas: 

1) DNS pattern options (summary):
   - Customer zone w/ A/CNAME -> customer IP/edge: customer-controlled; Redwood provides validation steps. Good for customer-proxied cases.
   - Customer zone w/ NS delegation -> Redwood resolver: customer creates NS records pointing to Redwood-managed nameservers (split-horizon); Redwood then manages per-tenant records. Good when customer wants Redwood to manage TTLs and rapid failover.

2) Certificate patterns (what we need):
   - Redwood-terminated (recommended for predictable latency): We require a formal CSR flow (machine-to-machine). We rotate certs on a 90-day cadence by default. We publish certificate SHA256 in the audit bucket. Automation: we expose a CSR endpoint (POST /v1/csr) and an API to accept cert bundles.
   - Customer-terminated / proxy: Customer must supply a cert chain and configure OCSP stapling or provide staple responses. If a customer uses mutual TLS for client-auth to their proxy, we will configure a TCP-level pass-through and not peek at the TLS layer.

3) SNI exceptions & routing: 
   - If we detect an SNI that matches a proxied tenant, we immediately route to a configured backend IP (customer appliance). That backend IP is stored in a per-tenant config (managed by customer via our onboarding portal or API).
   - Make sure customer-owned SANs do not overlap with Redwood-managed SANs for the same deployment stage (staging vs prod) to avoid routing ambiguity.

4) Audit & evidence requests: 
   - For Redwood-managed certs we can emit a per-rotation artifact: cert.pem, cert-chain.pem, thumbprint.txt and a rotation log entry. Customer-managed certs: customer must deposit a signed attestation or enable read-only access to the cert metadata bucket.

Gotcha examples: 
- If customers ask for wildcard certs to reduce ops, that raises risk for cross-tenant impersonation unless ACLs at the proxy layer are hardened. We can support but require customer-signed waiver.
- DNS TTLs: short TTLs help failover but increase query volume; recommend 60s for high-availability tenants or 300s otherwise.

I can attach a short sample CSR exchange payload and the exact API endpoints if that helps. Also happy to be on the call at 1pm PT.

—Karthik Iyer
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
